content: Many countries have developed essential medical care benefit packages that typically include immunization and other maternal and child health-care interventions. These services are delivered either at fixed health facilities or through outreach programs. Integrating health programs into common delivery systems enhances efficiency by sharing costs and, more importantly, increases the accessibility of life-saving interventions for the population. The integration of vaccine supply chains with other health commodity supply chains has been explored as a strategy to improve efficiency and impact. For example, Nepal successfully integrated all Ministry of Health logistics activities under a single entity, including procurement, forecasting, storage, distribution, and requisitioning across multiple programs. This integration took several years to achieve its intended outcomes but is now considered a model of effective integration. Conversely, Mali's attempt to integrate family planning into the essential medicines program without adequate planning led to poor availability and system disruptions. A framework for decision-making on supply chain integration has been developed, emphasizing that integration is not a one-size-fits-all solution and requires careful consideration of country-specific contexts. The goal is to maintain the uninterrupted availability of quality vaccines from manufacturers to service delivery points, ensuring no vaccination opportunities are missed due to stockouts. This requires adherence to the six rights of supply chain management: the right product, place, quantity, time, condition, and cost. Certain products, such as deworming tablets, vitamin A supplements, and iron tablets for children, are well-suited for integration with vaccine supply chains due to their similar target populations and distribution schedules. Other products, like HIV test kits and oxytocin (used to prevent postpartum hemorrhage), also present strong cases for integration due to their temperature-controlled storage needs and predictable demand patterns. However, products with different storage or distribution requirements, such as bulky items or those with unpredictable demand, may pose challenges for integration. Home-based records (HBRs) play a critical role in documenting immunization services received by individuals, ensuring families and health workers are aware of vaccination history. HBRs can range from vaccination-only cards to comprehensive child health books that include growth charts, developmental milestones, and guidance on child health and nutrition. Integrated health booklets, such as those used in Mexico, document vaccination history across the lifespan and provide additional health promotion and disease prevention information. Integrated health service delivery has been shown to improve access, convenience, and efficiency. For example, combining immunization with other health interventions, such as vitamin A supplementation and deworming, during outreach sessions or campaigns has increased coverage and reduced costs. However, challenges such as competing priorities, logistical complexities, and potential disruptions to routine health services must be carefully managed. In humanitarian emergencies, vaccination programs can be critical in reducing avoidable deaths and disease. Decision frameworks have been developed to guide the prioritization and delivery of vaccines during emergencies, ensuring ethical and rational decision-making. Similarly, school-based immunization programs are increasingly important for reaching older children and adolescents with vaccines like HPV, as well as booster doses. Overall, integrating immunization with other health services requires careful planning, coordination, and adaptation to local contexts. Successful integration efforts often involve joint planning, training, and supervision, as well as robust monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. Lessons learned from country experiences, such as those in Honduras and Somalia, highlight the importance of effective coordination, timely supply management, and community engagement in achieving integrated health service delivery.
